memory-retrieval/testing-effect.reason: confirmed: the bias check the grader lacked clears tie-break 2. Yang et al. 2021 (222 classroom studies) find PEESE g = 0.475, 3PSM g = 0.461 and trim-and-fill 0 missing, against a raw g = 0.499 (10.1037/bul0000309). Rowland's retention-interval moderator matches the claim's "days or more" (at least 1 day: g = 0.69 [0.56, 0.81], k = 56). The grader's recall-vs-recognition exemption misreads Rowland's Table 1, though. Initial free-recall tests gave g = 0.29 [0.07, 0.52] (k = 36), no larger than recognition, and Yang's free-recall quizzes gave g = 0.238. Free-recall's own format therefore sits at the small end of "moderate".
memory-retrieval/testing-effect.helps_overclaim: free-recall (and its variants): the effect label is moderate, but meta-analytic subgroups for initial free-recall tests are smaller (Rowland g = 0.29 [0.07, 0.52]; Yang g = 0.238). The helps text states no size, so it does not overclaim; the lead may want effect small-to-moderate for free-recall specifically.

memory-retrieval/retrieval-feedback.reason: confirmed: three consistent read experiments support B, and Rowland's full-text feedback moderator (g = 0.73 with feedback vs 0.39 without; 10.1037/a0037559) agrees with the claim's direction; nothing found meets a tie-break.

memory-retrieval/hypercorrection.reason: confirmed: several consistent experiments from at least two labs, with no meta-analysis and no failed replication found, meet B; this is a supporting claim.

memory-retrieval/pretesting.reason: confirmed: four consistent sources meet B. A search found no failed large replication. Newer syntheses bound the effect to prequestioned material, which matches the claim as written. This is a supporting claim.

memory-retrieval/retrieval-before-review.reason: confirmed: Arnold & McDermott's isolated potentiation effect is backed by Rowland's feedback moderator (retrieval followed by re-presentation g = 0.73; 10.1037/a0037559), which is Series' retrieve-then-review pattern. The claim meets B, and it cannot reach A while Chan et al.'s moderators remain unread.

memory-retrieval/distributed-practice.reason: confirmed: a third meta-analysis tests Series' exact manipulation, spaced vs massed retrieval (Latimier, Peyre & Ramus 2021; 10.1007/s10648-020-09572-8). It finds g = 1.01 with moderate heterogeneity (I² = 49%), and g = 0.74 [0.55, 0.91] after trim-and-fill, so no tie-break applies.

memory-retrieval/spacing-gap-ratio.reason: downgraded B→C: Cepeda et al. 2008's own 35-day condition replaces the grader's 3–6-day interpolation (10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02209.x). For retention intervals of 7, 35, 70 and 350 days, "the optimal gaps ... were 1, 11, 21, and 21 days" for recall, and 7 days for recognition at 35 days. For a one-month target, the 1-day and 3-day gaps therefore fall well short of the optimum, on the costly short side. The claim's second sentence rests on one study, and that study partly contradicts it.

memory-retrieval/expanding-vs-uniform.reason: confirmed: Latimier et al. 2021, now read, finds "no significant difference between expanding and uniform spacing schedules of retrieval practice (g = 0.034)" (10.1007/s10648-020-09572-8), which leaves the claim as written unsupported at C.
